pages.x: Britain's prisons were overflowing, and since American independence it could no longer ship convicts to America. In 1786 the government chose Botany Bay, on the east coast of Australia, which James Cook had charted in 1770.

In May 1787 eleven ships left Portsmouth under Captain Arthur Phillip with some 1,400 people, about 750 of them convicts. The youngest convict was a boy of nine, the oldest a woman of about 80. The voyage took eight months.
Botany Bay proved to be poor land, so on 26 January 1788 Phillip landed at a deeper harbour to the north, Sydney Cove, raised the British flag and claimed the land for King George III.

The land was the country of the Eora and other Aboriginal peoples, whose ancestors had lived in Australia for more than 50,000 years. The British took it as if it belonged to no one, and the Eora resisted the loss of their land and food.
In 1789 smallpox broke out among the Aboriginal people around Sydney, who had no resistance to it. Officers found bodies in caves and on the beaches.

pages.x: Phillip had an Eora man, Bennelong, captured so the British could learn the language and ways of his people. Bennelong escaped, came back on his own terms and became a go-between. In 1792 he sailed to England with Phillip.

Others fought. Pemulwuy, a Bidjigal man, led attacks on the settlers for twelve years and was said to be proof against bullets after surviving many wounds. He was shot dead in 1802, and his head was sent to England.

The colony grew into modern Australia. 26 January is celebrated as Australia Day, but many Aboriginal Australians mark it as Invasion Day, a day of mourning. The country is still working out how to honour the oldest living cultures on Earth.
